body.heading: The first close look
paragraphs: In the 1600s, simple microscopes opened a door nobody knew existed. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch draper with a gift for grinding lenses, looked at pond water and found it full of tiny swimming creatures — the first bacteria ever seen.
Around the same time, Robert Hooke examined cork under a microscope and saw a honeycomb of little boxes. He called them “cells” — the word biologists still use today.

body.heading: Beams instead of light
paragraphs: Optical microscopes have a hard limit: light itself. Once details are smaller than the wavelength of light, no lens can separate them. The way past the limit was to stop using light at all.

Electron microscopes, developed in the 1930s, illuminate samples with beams of electrons, whose effective wavelength is far shorter. Suddenly viruses, cell machinery and the surfaces of materials stood revealed — in black and white, and often only after careful preparation, but unmistakably there.

body.heading: Why smaller matters
paragraphs: Almost everything in modern medicine leans on these tools. Germ theory, antibiotics, vaccines and microchips all began with someone seeing something that had always been too small to see.
The lesson repeats at every scale: when a new instrument arrives, a new world tends to follow.

takeaway: Each new way of seeing — lenses, then electron beams — opened a smaller world that changed medicine and science.
